analysis.one_liner: Lets each state cap credit card and consumer loan interest rates for its own residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Banking Committee after being referred there in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a credit card company can charge a borrower in any state the rate allowed in the state where the card issuer is headquartered — often a state with no interest rate cap. This bill would change that for credit cards, installment loans, and other consumer credit (not home mortgages): the annual percentage rate, including fees, could not exceed whatever maximum rate the borrower's own home state allows. States could then enforce their own rate limits against lenders anywhere in the country.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers in states with low or no tolerance for high interest rates, who would get their home state's rate cap enforced against out-of-state lenders. State governments and attorneys general, whose consumer-protection authority would be restored after decades of being overridden.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Truth in Lending Act so that the annual percentage rate on any consumer credit transaction other than a home mortgage — including fees folded into the rate — cannot exceed the maximum rate the borrower's home state permits [S2] [S3].

Because the cap applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law', it would override the current rule that lets national banks charge rates exported from the state where they are chartered, restoring states' ability to protect their own residents [S3].
The bill was introduced by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse with Sen. Richard Durbin and drew cosponsors from three Senate Democrats and the Senate's sole Independent [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and other consumer lenders, whose current freedom to charge rates unlimited by the borrower's home state would end. In states without caps, some borrowers could also face tighter credit access as issuers reprice or restrict lending to riskier customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

drawbacks.text: Many states set no rate caps at all, so the bill would protect borrowers unevenly — a consumer in a state with no maximum rate would see no change, leaving a patchwork rather than a national ceiling [S2].
Hard interest rate caps tend to reduce credit availability to higher-risk borrowers: lenders cannot price for risk, so they may deny credit or cut off cardholders rather than lend at the capped rate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given states real power to stop out-of-state lenders from charging whatever they want, a meaningful consumer protection, at the real cost that borrowers with poor credit might lose access to some cards and loans in capped states. Its main weakness is structural: it defers to whatever each state decides, so millions of borrowers in states without caps would be no better off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read and referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Whitehouse, joined by Sen. Durbin, introduced the bill in the Senate on January 15, 2009 [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1] [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and national banks that profit from charging rates untethered to the borrower's home state are better off, since nothing limited them. State attorneys general and borrowers in states with rate caps did not get back the enforcement power the bill would have restored.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers and national banks

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the same party's majority — it never came to a vote, so no partisan split on the merits is on the record.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and national banks
industries.note: Their business model depends on charging rates set in low-cap charter states like South Dakota and Delaware, regardless of the borrower's home state. The bill would have ended that export of rates for consumer credit, directly cutting into interest and fee revenue.
These lenders charge rates far above most state caps. A home-state cap enforced against any lender would have closed the route they and their bank partners use to operate around state limits.

industries.industry: State governments and consumer protection agencies
industries.note: States would regain the power to enforce their own rate limits against out-of-state lenders, restoring consumer-protection authority they lost when courts let national banks export rates.
